svg.title: Betterleaks keeps a detected secret out of the CI log, and shows more only on the developer's machine: the CI log prints REDACTED, and the developer's own terminal shows more on request
svg.text: Betterleaks keeps a detected secret out of the CI log,
and shows more only on the developer's machine
Scenario: the CI log prints REDACTED, and the developer's own terminal shows more on request
Every scan hides the whole value unless told otherwise
The shared CI log never prints the value
The developer sees more in their own terminal only

g.text: Given GitLab shows that the generated project hides 100 percent of a detected value by
default
GitLab shows the generated .config/betterleaks/Taskfile.yml on the main branch. Line 8, highlighted, sets
TASK_BETTERLEAKS_REDACT to "100" unless the developer gives another value.
The number is the share of a detected value, in percent, that a Betterleaks scan hides from its output. The test also
checks that all six scans (full, staged and branch, each in a container or from the binary) receive 100.
When a developer pushes a branch with a synthetic password in it
A developer commits a made-up password in src/service.js on a new branch and pushes it. GitLab shows the file on the
branch feature/synthetic-password, the whole value on line 1.
Hiding a value protects what a scan prints, not the repository: the password stays in the file until someone removes it.
Then the Betterleaks job fails on GitLab and its log prints REDACTED instead of the password
The developer opens a merge request. Its pipeline runs the generated code:betterleaks job, with no setting changed, and
the job fails. GitLab shows the job page, its log scrolled to what the scan found.
The finding names the rule generic-password, the file src/service.js and line 1, and prints "REDACTED" where the
password was. Everyone on the project can read this log, so the value stays out of it.
Then the developer's terminal shows the first 12 characters of the password with the setting
at 25
To see what was caught, the developer runs the same scan in their clone, with TASK_BETTERLEAKS_REDACT=25 in the
environment. The scan hides the last quarter of the value: line 1 shows the first 12 of its 16 characters, then "...".
The scan still fails.
And the developer's terminal shows the whole password with the setting at 0
The same scan with TASK_BETTERLEAKS_REDACT=0 after the command hides nothing: line 1 shows the whole value.
Both runs stay on this machine: nothing is committed and nothing reaches GitLab. The test also checks that all six scans
accept both ways of setting the value.
